title: Alignment of Security Function to Business Strategy
description: How security governance aligns the security function with the organization's business goals.

nodes.title: Corporate Governance
nodes.description:
The rules, practices and processes that direct and control an organization toward its goals, usually to increase its value.
Keeps everyone in the organization aligned on the same goals.

children.title: Security Governance
children.description:
The rules, practices and processes that direct and control the security function, so that security is aligned with the organization's goals.
Security should be an enabler for the business.
Instead of just saying no, explain the risks and the ways to reduce them.

children.title: Focus of Security
children.description:
Security exists to help the organization reach its goals.
Its two aims: let the business do what it needs to do, and make the organization worth more.

children.title: Enable Business
children.description: Security should help the business do what it needs to do, not stand in its way.

children.title: Increase Value
children.description: Security should make the organization worth more, not be seen only as a cost center.

children.title: Clearly Defined Roles & Responsibilities
children.description: People must know exactly what they own and must answer for, and which tasks they must carry out.

children.title: Accountability
children.description:
Ownership: ultimate answerability, blameworthiness and liability. Where the buck stops.
Cannot be delegated or outsourced.
The asset owner stays accountable even when someone else does the work.

children.title: Responsibility
children.description:
Can be delegated. The party doing the work implements and enforces controls as directed by the accountable party.
Example: a cloud provider stores, processes and secures customer data, but the customer stays accountable for it.

children.title: Due Care
children.description: Protecting assets responsibly, based on the organization's goals and objectives: doing what a reasonable, prudent person would do in the same situation.

children.title: Due Diligence
children.description:
Being able to prove to stakeholders that assets are being protected responsibly.
Stakeholders include management, regulators, customers and shareholders.

children.title: Import/export controls
children.description:
Laws that restrict selling or shipping certain technologies to other countries, including some cryptographic algorithms and systems.
These laws followed advances in cryptography in the 1970s and 1980s, such as DES and asymmetric cryptography.
Violations can carry serious penalties, including federal prison.

children.title: ITAR & EAR
children.description:
Two US regulations that restrict the manufacture, sale and distribution of specific technologies, including some cryptography:
- the first covers military items: defense articles, technical data and defense services
- the second covers dual-use items not covered by the first, and some defense-related items
Full names: International Traffic in Arms Regulations; Export Administration Regulations.

children.title: Wassenaar Arrangement
children.description:
A voluntary, multinational export control regime, not a strict law.
42 participating countries.
Members exchange information on transfers of conventional weapons and dual-use goods and technologies.

children.title: Transborder data flow
children.description:
Data residency (data localization) laws that restrict data from leaving a country.
Example: a law that requires citizens' personal data to be stored inside the country.

children.title: Privacy
children.description:
Protecting personal information, and letting people control what others know about them.
You cannot achieve privacy without security.
Covered in its own mind map.

children.title: Ethics
children.description:
Organizations should write their ethics into policy.
Ethics is based on doing nothing that harms anyone else.

children.title: (ISC)² Code of Professional Ethics
children.description:
Every CISSP must agree to this code. Expect it on the exam.
The four canons are applied in order: when they conflict, the earlier canon wins.
1. Protect society, the common good, necessary public trust and confidence, and the infrastructure.
2. Act honorably, honestly, justly, responsibly, and legally.
3. Provide diligent and competent service to principals.
4. Advance and protect the profession.

children.title: Corporate Laws
children.description:
Policies act as the organization's internal rules: they tell people what they must do.
They range from the overarching security policy down to standards, procedures, baselines and guidelines.

children.title: Overarching Security Policy
children.description:
The organization's overall approach to security.
Issued and supported by the Board and senior management.
Sets the security goals and keeps security aligned with business goals.

children.title: Functional Security Policies
children.description:
Detailed policies for specific areas, such as access control, encryption, incident response and data backups.
Example: every laptop must have malware protection.

children.title: Standards
children.description:
Mandatory hardware or software mechanisms.
Example: one specific antivirus product is required on all Windows laptops.

children.title: Procedures
children.description:
Mandatory step-by-step instructions.
Example: the steps to install and configure the required antivirus.

children.title: Baselines
children.description:
Minimum security levels and mandatory configurations.
Example: a Windows laptop checklist: host firewall on, patches applied, antivirus configured.

children.title: Guidelines
children.description:
Recommendations, not mandatory.
Example: use MFA for admin accounts, while some systems cannot support it yet.

children.title: Risk Management
children.description:
A critical tool for protecting assets with limited resources: value the assets, analyze the risks and treat them. Part of security governance.
Covered in its own mind map.

children.title: Procurement
children.description:
Involve security from the start of buying anything.
Validate the business requirements first.
For services, document the security requirements in the SLR (Service Level Requirements) and use it to evaluate providers.

children.title: Contracts & SLAs
children.description:
After a provider is chosen, the SLR is turned into the provider's formal service commitments, added as an addendum to the legally binding agreement with the provider.
Together they describe the service, its targets and each party's responsibilities.
Responsibility can be outsourced. Accountability cannot.
Full name: Service Level Agreement.

children.title: Awareness, Training & Education
children.description:
Everyone is responsible for security, but people need to know what that means for them. Three levels, from least to most formal:
- informal communication, such as emails and posters, to change culture. Example: posters that warn staff about phishing.
- semi-formal teaching of specific skills. Example: how to deploy a particular firewall.
- teaching fundamental concepts. Example: a CISSP course.
